children: The rare procedure enabled treatment of severe aortic stenosis in a high-risk patient while avoiding iodinated contrast and protecting transplanted kidney function

Apollo Hospitals, Bannerghatta Road, Bengaluru, has performed a rare zero-contrast Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) on a 68-year-old kidney transplant recipient, enabling treatment of severe aortic stenosis without using iodinated contrast dye. The procedure was performed in September 2026 on a patient considered too high-risk for conventional intervention at multiple centres.

The 39-kg patient had undergone a kidney transplant in 1999 and was living with a progressively deteriorating transplanted kidney. He subsequently developed severe aortic stenosis, which restricted blood flow through the heart and was compounded by severe frailty, heavily calcified blood vessels and dissected femoral arteries.

Conventional TAVR typically uses iodinated contrast to visualise blood vessels and guide valve placement. However, contrast exposure can further impair kidney function in patients with advanced renal disease or a transplanted kidney. Apollo’s Structural Heart team therefore planned the intervention without contrast, using MRI, vascular ultrasound and fluoroscopic guidance.

“This was one of the most technically demanding structural heart procedures we have performed,” said Dr Srinivasa Prasad, Senior Consultant Interventional Cardiologist, Apollo Hospitals, Bannerghatta Road, Bengaluru.

“The challenge was not only replacing the patient's severely diseased heart valve but doing so without compromising his transplanted kidney. Zero-contrast TAVR demands meticulous planning, advanced imaging and seamless collaboration between cardiologists, imaging specialists and nephrologists,” he added.

The procedure was completed using exactly 0 mL of contrast dye. Following the intervention, blood flow through the replacement valve was restored while renal function remained stable. The patient’s breathing improved within 8-12 hours as fluid accumulation in the lungs resolved. He was able to walk the next day and was discharged three days after the procedure.

Post-procedure echocardiography showed normal valve function, while creatinine levels showed early improvement. At the one-month follow-up, the patient reported relief from cardiac symptoms, maintained healthy urine output and had not required dialysis. The case highlights the role of multimodality imaging, detailed procedural planning and collaboration between cardiology, nephrology, imaging and anaesthesia teams in managing complex structural heart cases.
